Q: When or why should I use numpy.meshgrid (Ny,Nx) arrays instead of two (1,Nx) and (Ny,1) arrays? A:

When to use np.meshgrid

You should usually use np.meshgrid when using coordinates, since it is better for plotting, and easier to index. This is because when you use np.meshgrid each coordinate in a plot is represented as (x[i, j], y[i, j], z[i, j]). When you do not use np.meshgrid it is not immediately clear whether a coordinate is represented as (x[i], y[j], z[i, j]) or (x[i], y[j], z[j, i]). This is why plotting libraries like matplotlib expect xx, yy and zz as arguments for 3D plots.

When to not use np.meshgrid

You should use tricks like in your example when making expansive calculations where you make use of different array sizes and eg. sum over different axes at different points. I would however suggest using np.newaxis instead of np.reshape to make your code more readable. This makes it clear which axis belongs to the x data and which belongs to the y data in your final result. This would look like this:

x = np.array([1,2,3,4,5])[np.newaxis, :]
y = np.array([6,7,8])[:, np.newaxis]

For more complex examples this makes it much easier to see whether it compiles and what happens. In this meaningless example:

x = np.array([1,2,3,4,5])
y = np.array([6,7,8])

np.sum(x[:, np.newaxis]*y[np.newaxis, :], axis=1)[:, np.newaxis] + np.sum(x[:, np.newaxis]*y[np.newaxis, :], axis=0)[np.newaxis, :]

It is pretty doable to deduce that the final shape will be (Nx, Ny), while this would be much harder when using np.reshape.

Performance speed

For performance speed it doesn't really matter. If there is a lot of calculations done on x and y separately, it is slower with np.meshgrid, but when there is a lot of calculations combining x and y, it is faster with np.meshgrid. For example, in your example the first option is faster, but when you do not square x and y first, then meshgrid is faster.

Q: Formatting seconds in std::chrono A:

Your variable now uses std::chrono::system_clock::duration, which is not seconds. On your system, it appears to be nanoseconds.

So in the line below, floor() is casting now to a different type that uses seconds, but assignment back to now casts it again to its original type using nanoseconds:

now = std::chrono::floor<std::chrono::seconds>( now );

You could instead do this, if you want what's printed to have seconds resolution:

std::format( "{0:%H:%M:%S}", std::chrono::floor<std::chrono::seconds>( now ) )

The lesson: Your now and now1 are different types. Only now1 is a type that truncates to seconds.

Q: Is there any way to git checkout previous branch? A:

From the release notes for 1.6.2

@{-1} is a way to refer to the last branch you were on. This is
accepted not only where an object name is expected, but anywhere a branch name is expected and acts as if you typed the branch name.
E.g. git branch --track mybranch @{-1}, git merge @{-1}, and
git rev-parse --symbolic-full-name @{-1} would work as expected.

and

git checkout - is a shorthand for git checkout @{-1}.

To see the list of previous checkouts:

i=0; while [ $? -eq 0 ]; do i=$((i+1)); echo -n "$i. "; git rev-parse --symbolic-full-name @{-$i} 2> /dev/null; done

This Bash one-liner script is not perfect but it should work for most cases. Note that sometimes the number may skip.

Tip: You can add it to .bashrc as a function.

Q: Safely storing and accessing EEPROM A:

Nigel Jones has covered some of the basics in your reference. There are plenty of alternatives.

One alternative, of you have lots of room, is storing key-value pairs instead of structures. Then you can update one value (by appending it) without erasing everything. This is most useful in devices that have a limited number of erase cycles. Your read routine will need to scan from the beginning, updating values each time the key is encountered. Of course your update routine will need to have a "garbage collector" that kicks in when the memory is full.

To handle device errors and power-downs in the middle of updates, we usually store multiple copies of the data. The simplest approach is to pingpong between to halves of the device using sequence number to determine which is newer. A CRC on each section is used to validate it. This also addresses the uninitialized data issue.

For the key-value version you'd need to append the new CRC after each write.

Q: How to rebase a branch with heavy changes onto a branch that moved the target directory? A:

Find the place where both branches diverged and create a temp branch there:

git checkout -b temp $( git merge-base main work )

Run the same rename that was carried out in main without any adjustments in content of the files:

test -d app || mkdir app # create the directory if it does not exist
git mv backend app/backend
git commit -m "moving all files"

Now, run the rebase of the work branch on top of this branch:

git branch separate-work work # let's work on a separate branch, just in case
git rebase temp separate-work # assuming it is a straight line so no additional options are being passed down to the rebase

Separate work should be just like work but all changes should be taking place at the new location of the files, right? Now rebase separate-work past temp and git should have no problem with files having being moved in main:

git rebase --onto main temp separate-work

If you like the result, place work on top of this and it should be fine.
